title: PRINCE2 principles, practices and processes refresher
blurb: Recognize which PRINCE2 Project Management practice or process a scenario event belongs to, seen through the agile lens.
question: Callowmere's registrar asks for the early-warning feature to be added to Release 1, changing the project backlog. Which PRINCE2 practice handles this, and why?

teach.body: Formally: PRINCE2 Agile combines PRINCE2 Project Management's principles, practices and processes with the agile mindset, frameworks, artifacts, techniques and workshops. PRINCE2 Project Management has five integrated elements: principles, people, practices, processes and the project context. In plain English: nothing from PRINCE2 is thrown away; each part is kept and tailored for agile delivery, so you still need to know what each practice and process is for.

teach.caption: PRINCE2 Agile covers all three areas while keeping governance and control throughout.

teach.h: The seven practices: the question each answers

teach.caption: Directing a project runs from the end of starting up to closure: the board decides and delegates day-to-day management to the PM.

head: If the stem says...
Process

Key decisions, overall control, day-to-day delegated
Assign and monitor work, keep within tolerance

Review the stage, approve the next stage plan

teach.body: The book names five characteristics that set a project apart from business as usual; they include change (it introduces change), temporary, cross-functional and unique. PRINCE2 Project Management can host any delivery method, but PRINCE2 Agile is specifically for iterative and incremental (agile) delivery. Performance targets cover benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk.

At Callowmere University, project manager Jamal Hussain knows PRINCE2 7 well. In starting up, the pro vice-chancellor leads the project canvas to show the hub is viable and worthwhile. Initiation fixes foundations before the £950,000 is committed. When the academic registrar asks for early warning in Release 1, that moves an epic into Release 1's approved scope and changes the project backlog: an issue handled formally. If the burn-up forecasts Welcome Week Musts slipping, progress triggers an exception.

teach.text: Classic traps: 'control changes to the baseline' is issues, but 'control deviations causing an exception' is progress. 'Before committing significant expenditure' is initiating; 'viable and worthwhile' is starting up. Practices, not themes, and the issues practice, not a change theme. In the Agile book the practice is spelt organization.

items: Five integrated elements: principles, people, practices, processes, project context.
Practices keep their PRINCE2 purpose and gain agile artifacts (canvas, release map, backlogs, dashboards).
Process hooks: viable and worthwhile (SU); before significant spend (IP); PM to team link (MPD); approve next stage plan (SB).
PRINCE2 Agile covers direction, management and delivery while keeping governance.

summary: You can now place an event in an agile scenario within the right PRINCE2 Project Management practice or process, using each one's purpose. You can also explain how PRINCE2 Agile keeps those elements and tailors them with agile artifacts and workshops.

A.q: Callowmere University's pro vice-chancellor has just received the mandate for the Student Support Hub. Before any initiation work, she leads a project canvas workshop so that the university can judge whether the hub is viable and worthwhile. Which process is the project in?
A.why: Starting up a project ensures the prerequisites for initiating are in place by answering whether there is a viable and worthwhile project; the executive leads the project canvas here (13.2.1, Table 13.1).

whyNot.0: Initiating comes next and lays foundations before significant expenditure.
whyNot.1: Directing is the board's process of decisions and control, starting after starting up.
whyNot.3: A stage boundary reviews a completed stage; no stage has run yet.

A.q: During stage 2 of Callowmere's project, the academic registrar asks for the early-warning feature, planned for Release 3, to be added to Release 1. Adding it would change the project backlog. Which practice provides the mechanism for handling this request?
A.why: The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the project's baseline; moving an epic into Release 1's approved scope changes the project backlog, a baseline change handled formally (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Risk handles uncertainties that may affect objectives, not requests to change the baseline.
whyNot.1: Progress compares actuals with plans and controls deviations causing an exception.
whyNot.2: Plans define what is to be delivered, how and when; the release map may be updated after the decision.

A.q: Callowmere's council has fixed the budget at £950,000. Before most of it is spent, Jamal Hussain and the team agree the project backlog, the release map and the management approaches, and assemble them for the board. Which process is this?
A.why: Initiating a project establishes solid foundations so the business understands the work needed before committing to significant expenditure (13.4.1).

whyNot.1: Starting up asks whether the project is viable and worthwhile, before initiation.
whyNot.2: Controlling a stage assigns and monitors work once a delivery stage is under way.
whyNot.3: Directing is the board's decision-making; the PM's foundation work sits in initiating.

B.q: Midway through stage 2 at Callowmere, the burn-up chart forecasts that self-referral and booking, both Must haves, will not be ready before Welcome Week within the fixed budget. Which practice provides the mechanism for forecasting this and controlling the resulting exception?
B.why: Progress monitors actual achievements against plans, provides a forecast and controls any deviations causing an exception (12.1, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Issues controls changes to the baseline; the deviation here is a forecast breach.
whyNot.2: Risk handles uncertainties before they happen; the forecast breach needs progress control.
whyNot.3: Quality covers users' requirements and how they are met, not forecasting against tolerance.

B.q: Callowmere's quality team wants evidence that each release has been tested with real students. The web team agrees acceptance criteria with the student design panel and records them with the stories in its product backlog. Which practice is MOST clearly applied?
B.why: Quality documents users' requirements of the project's products and establishes how they will be met (9.1); in agile, the product backlog holds stories and links to the team DoD.

whyNot.0: The business case judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable.
whyNot.1: Plans define what will be delivered, how and when, not the acceptance criteria users need.
whyNot.3: Organization sets up accountability and responsibilities.

B.q: Northmere Systems' team accepts a set of user stories for the records link from Jamal Hussain, agrees how it will report through its team dashboard, delivers the stories and notifies completion. Which process covers this work?
B.why: Managing product delivery controls the link between the project manager and the delivery team, agreeing requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery (13.6.1).

whyNot.1: Controlling a stage is the PM's process of assigning and monitoring work; the team's side is managing product delivery.
whyNot.2: A stage boundary reviews a completed stage and approves the next stage plan.
whyNot.3: Initiating lays the project's foundations; delivery work comes later.

C.q: Jamal Hussain proposes skipping initiation because the web team will 'work things out in sprints', and asks the council to release the whole budget straight after starting up. Is this an appropriate application of the PRINCE2 processes, and why?
options: Yes, because agile teams plan their work iteratively in sprints
Yes, because the council has already fixed the overall budget
No, because initiating sets foundations before significant spend
No, because starting up a project is where the PID is produced
C.why: Initiating a project establishes solid foundations so the business understands the work before committing to significant expenditure (13.4.1); agile tailors it, it does not remove it.

whyNot.0: Sprints plan delivery at team level; they do not replace the project's foundations.
whyNot.1: A fixed budget still needs initiation before it is committed.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the PID is assembled in initiation.

C.q: At the end of Release 1, Callowmere's board reviews how the stage went, looks at the updated release map, approves it as the plan for the next stage and confirms the business justification. Is this an appropriate application of 'managing a stage boundary', and why?
options: Yes, because closing a project confirms acceptance at each release
Yes, because the boundary lets the board approve the next stage plan
No, because release maps are updated in the team planning workshop
No, because the next stage plan is approved by the project manager
C.why: Managing a stage boundary gives the board information to review the stage, review the updated release map, approve the next stage plan and confirm continued justification (13.7.1).

whyNot.0: Closing a project happens once, at the end; this is a stage boundary.
whyNot.2: Team planning workshops produce detailed team plans; stage boundaries produce high-level release map updates.
whyNot.3: The project board approves the next stage plan.

C.q: Jamal Hussain tells the web team that PRINCE2 Agile replaces PRINCE2's practices with Scrum, so the risk register and issue register will not be needed. Is this an appropriate view of how PRINCE2 Agile works, and why?
options: Yes, because Scrum provides sprints and retrospectives instead
Yes, because agile embraces change, so issues need no record
No, because Scrum events cannot be used on a PRINCE2 Agile project
No, because PRINCE2 Agile keeps each practice and tailors it for agile
C.why: PRINCE2 Agile is PRINCE2 Project Management's principles, practices and processes tailored with agile frameworks, artifacts and techniques; the risk and issue registers remain (3.1, Table 10.1, 11.3.4).

whyNot.0: Scrum events support delivery but do not provide governance such as risk and issue control.
whyNot.1: Change is embraced, but baseline changes are still captured and controlled.
whyNot.2: Agile frameworks such as Scrum are used within PRINCE2 Agile.

reteach.title: Purpose finds the practice or process
reteach.question: Can you place a scenario event in the right PRINCE2 practice or process?

blocks.body: Practices answer standing questions: why (business case), who (organization), what and when (plans), what users need (quality), what if (risk), what now when things change (issues), are we on track (progress). Processes are moments in the life cycle: viable and worthwhile, foundations, control, delivery, boundary, closure.

head: Phrase
Answer
rows: Link between PM and delivery team

blocks.text: PRINCE2 Agile keeps every practice and process; it tailors them with agile artifacts, techniques and workshops.

explain.body: Project management is strong on direction and management but gives little focus to product delivery. Agile is strong on product delivery but light on direction and management. PRINCE2 Agile covers all three with governance throughout.

test.q: Callowmere's web team has strong Scrum skills, but the university has struggled to govern past digital projects. In which area of a project is agile, on its own, strongest?
test.why: Agile is strong on product delivery and responding to change but light on direction and management (Figure 3.1, 3.1).

whyNot.1: Project direction is where project management, not agile, is strong.
whyNot.2: Project management is where PRINCE2 is strong; agile is light here.
whyNot.3: This is not one of the three areas in Figure 3.1.

explain.body: Organization defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities: the who. Plans cover what, how, where, when and how much. Business case covers why.

test.q: Jamal Hussain agrees with the board who will be chief product owner, which product owner leads each team and who provides project assurance. Which practice is he applying?
test.why: Organization defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities (7.1).

whyNot.0: Plans define products and the means to deliver them.
whyNot.2: The business case judges whether the project is worthwhile.

explain.body: The project board is accountable for success. It makes the key decisions and exercises overall control, and delegates day-to-day management to the project manager.

test.q: Callowmere's board receives the project dashboard, gives ad hoc direction when Jamal asks for advice, and leaves day-to-day management to him. Which process is the board performing?
test.why: Directing a project enables the board to be accountable by making key decisions and exercising overall control while delegating day-to-day management to the PM (13.3.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage is the PM's process.
whyNot.1: The stem describes ongoing direction during a stage, not a boundary review.
whyNot.2: Starting up happens before the board directs the project.

explain.body: Among the characteristics of a project: it introduces change, it is temporary, it is cross-functional and it is unique. Business as usual is repetitive and ongoing, and it adopts the change and the benefits once the project ends.

test.q: Callowmere's hub team brings together university web developers, Northmere's integration developers and wellbeing practitioners from two campuses. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST show?
test.why: Projects are cross-functional: teams span functional divisions and sometimes organizations (1.3.1).

whyNot.0: Temporary means having a start and an end.
whyNot.1: Unique means a different team, customer, product or timeframe from before.
whyNot.3: Change means the project introduces the change that BAU identified.
